title: Say the Digits You See
statement:
Build a sequence of digit strings. The first term is "1". Every later term describes the previous one out loud.

To describe a term, split it into runs of the same digit standing next to each other. For each run, from left to right, write the length of the run and then the digit. Glue the pieces together.

For example, "3322251" has runs 33, 222, 5, 1, so it is described as "23" + "32" + "15" + "11" = "23321511".

Return the n-th term of the sequence that starts at "1".

examples.why: The first term is given, nothing to describe.

hints: There is no formula. Build term 2 from term 1, term 3 from term 2, and so on.
Describing one term is a run-length encoding: find where each run of equal digits starts and ends.
Keep a start index i. Move j right while s[j] equals s[i]. Append (j − i) and s[i], then set i = j. Build the result in an array and join it once.

explain.intuition:
Each step is plain run-length encoding with the count written before the digit. The only work is finding the runs, which is a two-pointer scan: i marks where a run starts and j walks until the digit changes. The run length is j − i.

Something you can mention in an interview: no run ever gets longer than 3, so every count is a single digit and the strings only use the digits 1, 2 and 3. The terms grow by about 30% each step, so term 30 has a few thousand characters. Collect pieces in an array and join once, the same way you would build a large HTML string, instead of concatenating in a loop.
steps: Repeat n − 1 times: set i = 0 and an empty parts list.
While i < s.length: move j from i while s[j] == s[i], push j − i and s[i], then set i = j.
Join the parts into the new s.
pitfalls: Counting each digit over the whole string instead of per run. "1211" has three 1s, but they form two runs, so the answer is "111221", not "3112".
Forgetting to emit the final run after the loop when you track runs with a "digit changed" check.
Off by one on n: n = 1 means zero description steps.

solutions.title: Run-length scan, term by term
solutions.idea: Describe each term with two pointers marking the start and end of every run.

solutions.title: Group with a library helper
solutions.idea: Python's itertools.groupby and a regex with a back-reference in TypeScript both find the runs for you. Good to know, but be ready to write the scan by hand.

followups: Start from a different seed such as "3". Which properties of the sequence still hold?
Can you find the length of term 60 without building the string? (Hint: split terms into pieces that evolve independently.)
